facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(2): 'Where a marriage is solemnised by an authorised celebrant, not being a minister of religion, it is sufficient if each of the parties says to the other, in the presence of the authorised celebrant and the witnesses, the words: "I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)"; or words to that effect.'
facts.source_name: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: Quote exactly. The permitted forms are wife, husband or spouse, and 'thee' may be said as 'you' only because the Act allows 'words to that effect'; the celebrant decides what counts. Deciding authority: the authorised celebrant, under the Attorney-General's Department.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(1): where the authorised celebrant is a minister of religion, the marriage 'may be solemnised according to any form and ceremony recognised as sufficient for the purpose by the religious body or organisation of which he or she is a minister.'
facts.source_name: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: Religious ceremonies follow their own rite; couples ask their minister about adding funny or personal lines.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 46(1) (the monitum): where the authorised celebrant is not a minister of religion of a recognised denomination, the celebrant 'shall say to the parties, in the presence of the witnesses, the words: "I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law. Before you are joined in marriage in my presence and in the presence of these witnesses, I am to remind you of the solemn and binding nature of the relationship into which you are now about to enter. Marriage, according to law in Australia, is the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life."; or words to that effect.'
facts.source_name: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: Said by the celebrant, not the couple. Useful as the serious anchor before playful personal vows.

facts.claim: Attorney-General's Department: to get married in Australia you must, among other things, 'use specific words during the ceremony', give a notice of intended marriage form to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding, and be married by an authorised marriage celebrant. AGD says it 'can provide general guidance on marriage in Australia, but we can't give you specific legal advice' and directs couples to ask AGD or an authorised marriage celebrant.
facts.use_note: Deciding authority: the couple's authorised celebrant, with AGD's Marriage Law and Celebrants Section (1800 550 343) for general guidance.

facts.claim: Attorney-General's Department: since 12 June 2024 a celebrant must be physically present to solemnise a marriage, together with the parties and 2 witnesses. On the day, 3 marriage certificates are signed by the couple, the celebrant and 2 witnesses over 18; the celebrant lodges the paperwork with the state or territory registry of births, deaths and marriages within 14 days.

Marriage Act 1961 s 45(2) wording ends 'or words to that effect', and s 46(1) likewise. Nothing in s 45 or s 46 bars couples from adding their own vows; the Act sets the minimum words that must be said.
facts.source_name: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961
facts.use_note: The second sentence is our reading of the statute, not an AGD quote. AGD's Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for authorised celebrants (section 5.7, personalising vows) could not be read from an official URL this round; see N-01. Phrase as: 'personal vows go alongside the legal words, and your celebrant confirms the final wording'.

facts.claim: The Attorney-General's Department says overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant or registered in Australia, and an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here.
facts.use_note: Re-read 2026-11-19, wording unchanged. A ceremony abroad led by an Australian celebrant is symbolic unless the local legal process is also followed.

facts.claim: Legal at home, celebration abroad: the formal step is giving a Notice of Intended Marriage (NOIM) to an authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM can be witnessed remotely by audio-visual link, and AGD says 'You can complete it if you are overseas and plan to get married in Australia.'
facts.use_note: Present as an option: legal words said in Australia, funny personal vows can be repeated at a symbolic ceremony abroad.

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law.

Our Traditional Wedding Vows guide gives the Australian legal words as: 'I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, [name], take thee (or you), [name], to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse).' (Marriage Act 1961, s45(2)), and says civil celebrants must also say the monitum.
facts.source_name: Wedded Wonderland, Traditional Wedding Vows Word for Word
facts.use_note: Consistent with F-001 and F-003. Internal link for 'traditional vows'.

facts.claim: Our Traditional Wedding Vows guide: 'Civil celebrants and officiants: Very flexible, as long as the legal words are included.' 'Jewish, Hindu, Muslim and Sikh ceremonies: The core ritual stays. Personal vows can usually be added before or after it.' 'Civil celebrants usually let couples adjust the wording, as long as the legal words stay.' It also says that 'in almost every country you can say the traditional vows and meet the law, because the legal words either overlap with them or take ten seconds to add.'
facts.source_name: Wedded Wonderland, Traditional Wedding Vows Word for Word
facts.use_note: Our own guidance, not law. Pair with F-001/F-004 and tell couples their celebrant confirms the wording.

facts.claim: Our How Do You Write Your Own Wedding Vows guide (published 2026-09-29, updated 2026-10-27) suggests agreeing with your partner on length and whether vows 'should be romantic, funny, serious, or a mix', a six-step structure (partner's name, what you love, one story, 3 to 5 specific promises, the future, a strong closing), and 'A good target is 250 to 300 words, which usually takes about two minutes to read aloud.' It says the goal is to make vows 'personal enough to touch your partner, but not so private that they embarrass your guests', and that 'Reading from a card is completely fine'.
facts.source_name: Wedded Wonderland, How Do You Write Your Own Wedding Vows?
facts.use_note: Our guidance on length and structure. Note our Wedding Vows for Him page meta says 'keep them to about a minute'; reconcile wording (see N-03).

facts.claim: The same guide includes an original funny vow example that turns serious: it opens with a parallel parking joke, then says 'Behind the puns and the terrible sense of direction is the kindest person I know', and promises include 'I promise to laugh at your puns, even the ones that make me groan' and 'when life gets hard, I promise to show up with snacks, a hug, and a very bad joke of my own.'
facts.source_name: Wedded Wonderland, How Do You Write Your Own Wedding Vows?
facts.use_note: Model for the 'funny but meaningful' pattern. Do not reuse verbatim; link instead and write new examples.

facts.claim: Other Wedded Wonderland vow pages found by site map: Wedding Vows for Him With 30 Examples (/expert-advice/wedding-vows-for-him, 'romantic, funny, short or faith-led'), Wedding Vows for Her With 30 Examples by Tone and Length (/expert-advice/wedding-vows-for-her), Vow Renewal Vows: 12 Examples (/celebration-ideas/vow-renewal-vows), Catholic Wedding Vows Word for Word (/expert-advice/catholic-wedding-vows), and 10 Alternative Wedding Vows (/10-alternative-wedding-vows-that-will-have-everyone-in-tears), whose list opens 'To Split the Difference on the Thermostat'.
facts.use_note: Titles and descriptions from the site map only; bodies not read this round. Use as internal links.

facts.claim: Our real wedding feature 'Pink Heels, Forgotten Vows, and Golden Hours At The Grounds' quotes the bride: 'Both Billy and I couldn't say our wedding vows without messing them up. I think Billy called me his "woeful" wedded wife rather than lawful, and I forgot my name.'
facts.source_name: Wedded Wonderland real wedding, The Grounds of Alexandria
facts.use_note: Quote taken from the site map page description; confirm against the page body before quoting. A real published couple quote, usable as a light 'it is fine to fumble' moment with a link.

legal.summary: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(2): each party says 'I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)', or words to that effect, before a non-religious authorised celebrant and witnesses. Confirmed by the authorised celebrant / AGD.
s 45(1): ministers of religion use the form recognised by their religious body.
s 46(1): the civil celebrant says the monitum ('Marriage, according to law in Australia, is the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life.').
AGD: use specific words during the ceremony; NOIM 1 to 18 months ahead; married by an authorised celebrant.
Celebrant, couple and 2 witnesses physically present; certificates signed; lodged within 14 days.
Act sets minimum words 'or words to that effect'; personal vows sit alongside (our reading, medium).
Australian celebrants cannot perform overseas marriages; ceremony abroad led by them is symbolic.
NOIM 1 to 18 months; can be completed from overseas.
Overseas marriages not registrable in Australia but generally recognised.
